and priests and monks praying,
and weeping women wailing before her in groups.
Then a certain man from the Arabs became filled with zeal,
and threw a stone at the bier.
And the servants of the Amir Manaṣih, who were surrounding the bier like guards,
struck that Arab with a sword.
And a great uproar took place in Baghdad,
and many were killed among the Arabs and among the Christians.
And Abu Nasr, the husband of the deceased woman, fled to the house of Manaṣih, his master.
And the uproar did not cease until Abu Nasr was surrendered
and brought to the palace of the Caliph,
and was imprisoned for a short time.
And he was released,
and there was joy for the Christians.
And after a year, there were many locusts in the region of Baghdad,
so that they filled the earth,
and darkened the air,
and destroyed the trees and the crops.
And with drums and horns, the farmers drove them away from the crops.
And in the year 405,
405 of the Arabs,
Hakim, the Caliph of Egypt, commanded
that a woman should never be seen outside the door,
nor look out from a door, or from a window, or from a roof.
And he forbade the cobblers
from anyone sewing women's shoes at all.
And this law indeed he established
because he heard of the wantonness of the Egyptian women.
And at first he made for himself old women as spies,
who crept into houses and learned the secrets of the women,
and informed him
under what pretexts women were going out,
and how and where adulterous women met with adulterers.
And he would send a eunuch with soldiers to the house of whoever it was,
whether noble or lowly,
and they would say to him:
"Bring out to us so-and-so by name,"
whether she was his wife, or his sister, or his daughter;
and they would take her away.
And when he had gathered them together by fives and by tens,
he would drown them in the Nile, the great river.
And on this account the Egyptian women were humiliated,
and their secrets were exposed.
And the dread of him, more than that of Pharaoh, fell upon men and upon women.
And when the people had remained in this distress for seven years,
the chiefs of the neighborhoods wrote and informed Hakim,
saying: "Many women who are widows and bereaved of brothers and sons and relatives,
inside their doors are perishing from hunger and nakedness,
since they have no one who buys flax for them,
or who sells their handiwork or their yarn."
